title: The Motor Hierarchy: Planning, Executing, & Calibrating Movement
description: Trace motor commands from prefrontal intention to premotor sequencing, primary motor execution, corticospinal decussation, and upper vs. lower motor lesions.

slides.title: The Motor Hierarchy: From Goal to Action 🧗
slides.content:
# Organizing Voluntary Movement

Motor control is organized hierarchically across three descending cortical tiers:

1. **Prefrontal Cortex (Goal / Intention)**: Evaluates behavioral context and decides *what* to do (e.g., 'reach for that water glass').
2. **Premotor Cortex (PMC) & Supplementary Motor Area (SMA)**: Plans and sequences the complex spatio-temporal program of muscle activations needed.
   * *Mirror Neurons*: Discovered in premotor cortex (F5); fire both when performing a motor action and when passively observing another individual execute the same goal-directed action!
3. **Primary Motor Cortex (M1 - Precentral Gyrus)**: Executes the motor plan, sending descending action potentials down the corticospinal tract to spinal motor pools.

slides.title: The Corticospinal Tract & Pyramidal Decussation ⚡
slides.content:
## The Grand Motor Highway

* **Origin**: Large pyramidal Betz cells in cortical Layer V of M1.
* **Descent**: Axons travel through the internal capsule, cerebral peduncles, and pons into the **medullary pyramids**.
* **Pyramidal Decussation**:
  * **Lateral Corticospinal Tract (~90% of fibers)**: Crosses the midline (decussates) in the lower medulla; descends in the lateral spinal column to control **contralateral distal limb muscles** (independent finger movements, dexterity).
  * **Anterior Corticospinal Tract (~10% of fibers)**: Descends uncrossed; crosses at spinal levels to control bilateral **axial and trunk posture**.

quizData.question: Where does the lateral corticospinal tract cross the midline to control contralateral voluntary limb movement?

options.text: At the decussation of the pyramids in the caudal medulla

quizData.explanation: Approximately 90% of corticospinal axons cross to the opposite side at the pyramidal decussation in the caudal medulla.

slides.title: Upper vs. Lower Motor Neuron Lesions 🩺
slides.content:
## Clinical Neurology: Diagnosing Paralysis

| Clinical Sign | Upper Motor Neuron (UMN) Lesion (Cortex / Corticospinal) | Lower Motor Neuron (LMN) Lesion (Ventral Horn / Peripheral Nerve) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Muscle Tone** | **Hypertonia** / Spasticity ('clasp-knife' rigidity) | **Hypotonia** / Flaccidity |
| **Reflexes** | **Hyperreflexia** (clonus) | **Hyporeflexia** or Areflexia |
| **Babinski Sign** | **Positive** (Great toe extends upward, other toes fan) | **Negative** (Normal plantar flexion or absent) |
| **Muscle Atrophy** | Disuse atrophy only (mild, late) | Severe, rapid denervation **atrophy** and fasciculations |

slides.title: Neuroscience Pro Tip 💡
slides.content:
### The Babinski Reflex

Stroking the lateral sole of an infant's foot normally elicits a positive Babinski sign because corticospinal myelination is not yet mature. In an adult, a positive Babinski sign is a classic clinical red flag indicating corticospinal tract (UMN) damage from stroke, trauma, or multiple sclerosis.
